# records

A single-file utility that reads a semicolon-delimited CSV file and prints its
rows as a JSON array of objects on stdout.

## Layout

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `records.py` | The whole utility: `read_records(path)` plus a small CLI entry point. |
| `samples/visits.csv` | Sample input exercising the well-formed, short, and over-long row cases. |
| `docs/context.md` | Project context: invocation contract and data behavior in detail. |

## Invocation

```
python3 records.py <path-to-csv>
```

The path is required and positional; there are no flags. Output is one line of
JSON on stdout, and nothing is written back to the input file.

Run it against the bundled sample:

```
$ python3 records.py samples/visits.csv
[{"site": "north", "visits": "12", "active": "true"}, {"site": "south", "visits": "8", "active": null}, {"site": "west", "visits": "4", "active": "false", "surplus": ["manual", "checked"]}]
```

## Behavior in brief

- The delimiter is `;`, not `,`. The first line is the header and names the keys.
- Every value is emitted as a JSON string; no numbers or booleans are inferred.
- A row with too few fields gets `null` for the missing keys.
- A row with too many fields gets the surplus values as a list under `"surplus"`.

`docs/context.md` covers these cases, the error behavior, and the encoding
assumptions in full.

# Project context

Working notes on what `records.py` does and why its output looks the way it
does. Everything below was checked by running the utility under Python 3.9.6 on
macOS against `samples/visits.csv` and against throwaway inputs outside the
project.

## Invocation contract

```
python3 records.py <path-to-csv>
```

- Exactly one positional argument: the path to the input file. There are no
  options, no flags, and no stdin mode.
- On success the utility prints a single line of JSON to stdout and exits 0.
- The input file is opened read-only; the utility never writes to it.

Failures surface as uncaught Python tracebacks with a non-zero exit, not as
friendly messages:

- No argument at all raises `IndexError: list index out of range` from
  `sys.argv[1]`.
- A path that does not exist raises `FileNotFoundError`.

The whole file is parsed into a list before anything is printed, so memory use
scales with input size. That is fine at the sample's scale and worth
remembering before pointing it at a large export.

## Reading side

`read_records(path)` opens the file with `newline=""` and `encoding="utf-8"`,
then wraps it in `csv.DictReader(stream, delimiter=";", restkey="surplus")`.
Three choices in that line drive all of the interesting behavior:

- **`delimiter=";"`** — records are semicolon-separated. A comma is an ordinary
  character inside a value, so a comma-separated file parses as a single column.
- **`restkey="surplus"`** — values beyond the last header column are not
  dropped; they are collected under the key `"surplus"`.
- **`newline=""`** — required by the `csv` module so that quoted values may
  contain embedded newlines. Such a value comes through as one string with a
  `\n` inside it.

The header is the first line of the file and supplies the keys, in file order.
Standard CSV quoting applies, so `"a;b"` is one value containing a semicolon.

## Data behavior

Every value stays a string. `csv` performs no type inference and the script adds
none, so `12` becomes `"12"` and `true` becomes `"true"`. Any consumer that
wants numbers or booleans has to convert them itself.

Row-shape mismatches are tolerated rather than rejected, and the three cases are
exactly what `samples/visits.csv` demonstrates against the header
`site;visits;active`:

| Sample row | Shape | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `north;12;true` | matches the header | `{"site": "north", "visits": "12", "active": "true"}` |
| `south;8` | one field short | `{"site": "south", "visits": "8", "active": null}` |
| `west;4;false;manual;checked` | two fields long | `{"site": "west", "visits": "4", "active": "false", "surplus": ["manual", "checked"]}` |

Notes on those cases:

- Missing trailing fields become JSON `null`, because `DictReader`'s default
  `restval` is `None`. A `null` therefore means "the row was short", while `""`
  means "the field was present and empty" — the two are distinguishable.
- `"surplus"` is always a list, even when there is exactly one extra field.
- Because surplus values are positional leftovers, a row that merely skips a
  middle field shifts everything after it; `east;;2` under a two-column header
  yields `{"site": "east", "visits": "", "surplus": ["2"]}`. Nothing validates
  that a row is well-formed.
- A header column named `surplus` would collide with the overflow key. No
  current sample does this.

Other observed edge cases:

- An empty file and a header-only file both print `[]`.
- Blank lines in the body are skipped by `csv` and produce no record.
- `json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False)` means non-ASCII characters are printed
  literally as UTF-8 (`"café"`) rather than escaped (`"caf\u00e9"`).
- The file is read as `utf-8`, not `utf-8-sig`. A UTF-8 BOM is not stripped and
  ends up glued to the first header name, producing a key like `"﻿site"`.
  Inputs exported from spreadsheet tools are the likely way to hit this.

## Uncertain / not established

- There is no test suite, no dependency manifest, and no packaging metadata, so
  the supported Python versions are unstated. The code uses nothing newer than
  Python 3.6 and was exercised here on 3.9.6.
- The intended downstream consumer of the JSON is unknown, so it is unclear
  whether `null` fields and `surplus` lists are meant to be tolerated
  indefinitely or to be caught and reported later.

# Project context

## Purpose and scope

`records.py` converts one semicolon-delimited text file into a single JSON array
on stdout. It is the whole project: there is no package, no configuration file,
no test suite and no dependency beyond the Python standard library
(`csv`, `json`, `sys`).

Out of scope, as far as the supplied source shows: writing files, validating or
coercing field values, reporting data problems, and reading from stdin.

## Current state

Observed on 2026-09-28 by running the utility against the bundled sample under
CPython 3.9.6 on macOS. This is code-and-local-run evidence; there is no
deployment, packaging or CI in this project to describe.

### Invocation

```sh
python3 records.py <path>
```

- One positional argument, read directly as `sys.argv[1]`. There is no argument
  parser, no flags, and no `--help`.
- Called with no argument, it raises `IndexError` from line 10 and exits with a
  traceback rather than a usage message.
- Output is one JSON array on a single line, printed with `ensure_ascii=False`,
  so non-ASCII characters are emitted literally rather than escaped.
- The input is opened with `newline=""` and `encoding="utf-8"`.

### Data behavior

`read_records` wraps `csv.DictReader` with `delimiter=";"` and
`restkey="surplus"`, and materializes the result with `list(...)`, so the entire
file is held in memory at once.

- The first row is the header and supplies the JSON object keys.
- **Every value stays a string.** There is no type coercion: `12` becomes
  `"12"` and `true` becomes `"true"`.
- **Short rows** — fields the row does not supply become `null`. `restval` is
  left at its default of `None`, so the key is present with a null value rather
  than omitted.
- **Long rows** — values past the last header column are collected into a list
  under the extra key `"surplus"`. That key appears only on rows that overflow.
- A header-only file produces `[]`.

The bundled sample covers all three row shapes:

```
site;visits;active
north;12;true
south;8
west;4;false;manual;checked
```

produces, reformatted here for reading (actual output is one line):

```json
[{"site": "north", "visits": "12", "active": "true"},
 {"site": "south", "visits": "8", "active": null},
 {"site": "west", "visits": "4", "active": "false",
  "surplus": ["manual", "checked"]}]
```

## Decisions and constraints

**Approved — `records.py` and `samples/visits.csv` must stay byte-identical.**
Authority: the project instructions in `CLAUDE.md` ("Preserve supplied code and
sample data") and the task request that established this documentation. The
sample is a fixture whose exact ragged shape is what makes it useful; editing it
to look tidy would destroy the coverage described above.

**Approved — do not commit.** Authority: `CLAUDE.md`. Changes are left in the
working tree for the user to review and commit themselves.

The implementation choices below are *observed in the source*, not recorded
decisions. No rationale for them is documented anywhere in this project, and the
author is not identified:

- semicolon rather than comma as the delimiter;
- `"surplus"` as the overflow key name;
- strings preserved rather than parsed into numbers or booleans.

Treat them as load-bearing until an owner says otherwise — a downstream consumer
may depend on any of them — but do not cite them as approved design intent.

## Open questions and next actions

- **Are ragged rows valid input or a data defect?** The utility accepts both
  short and long rows silently, and the sample enshrines them, but nothing
  records whether that tolerance is intentional or merely unhandled. This
  matters before anyone adds validation: the answer decides whether a short row
  should stay `null` or become an error. Needs an owner decision.
- **Is the `"surplus"` key name reserved?** Behavior when a header column is
  itself named `surplus` has not been tested. Unknown; check before relying on
  the key's uniqueness.
- No next actions are outstanding. Nothing in this project is blocked.

## Canonical references

- [`README.md`](README.md) — entry point and the invocation example.
- [`records.py`](records.py) — the full implementation, 11 lines.
- [`samples/visits.csv`](samples/visits.csv) — the ragged fixture.
- [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md) — project instructions and the context maintenance rule.

# Project context

## Purpose and scope

A single-file utility, [`records.py`](records.py), that reads a semicolon-delimited

stdout. [`samples/visits.csv`](samples/visits.csv) is the supplied fixture used to
exercise the parsing edge cases below.

Scope boundaries: there is no test suite, packaging, dependency manifest, CLI
argument parser, or output-file handling in the project. The utility performs no
type conversion and no validation; every parsed value is a string, `null`, or a
list of strings.

## Current state

Observed on 2026-09-28 by reading `records.py` and running it under Python 3.9.6
on macOS. No deployment or packaged release of this utility was examined, so its
distribution state is unknown.

### Invocation

```text
python3 records.py <path>
```

The path is read positionally from `sys.argv[1]`; there are no flags or options.
The file is opened with `newline=""` and `encoding="utf-8"`. Output is a single
line of JSON written to stdout with `ensure_ascii=False`, so non-ASCII characters
are emitted literally rather than escaped. The whole file is materialized into a
list in memory before anything is printed.

Error behavior is unhandled exceptions with exit status 1 and a traceback on
stderr — `IndexError` when no path argument is given, and `FileNotFoundError`
when the path does not exist (both observed).

### Data behavior

Parsing uses `csv.DictReader(stream, delimiter=";", restkey="surplus")`. The first
line is consumed as the header and supplies the object keys. The consequences,
each demonstrated by a row of the sample fixture:

- **Short rows** get `None` for the missing trailing columns, because `restval` is
  left at its default. Emitted as JSON `null`, not as an empty string or a
  dropped key.
- **Long rows** keep the header-named fields and collect every surplus value into
  a list under the key `surplus`. That key is absent from rows that are not long,
  so the objects in one output array are not guaranteed to share a key set.
- **No type coercion:** `12` stays `"12"` and `true` stays `"true"`.

Running the utility against the fixture produces (reformatted here for reading;
the real output is one line):

```json
[
  {"site": "north", "visits": "12", "active": "true"},
  {"site": "south", "visits": "8", "active": null},
  {"site": "west", "visits": "4", "active": "false",
   "surplus": ["manual", "checked"]}
]
```

The fixture covers the well-formed, short and long cases only. Behavior for
quoted fields, embedded delimiters or newlines, an empty file, a header-only
file, duplicate header names and non-UTF-8 bytes follows from `csv.DictReader`
and Python's defaults but has not been exercised here.

## Decisions and constraints

- **Constraint (owner instruction, [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md)):** `records.py` and
  `samples/visits.csv` are supplied material and must be preserved byte-for-byte.
  Document the observed behavior instead of "fixing" it. Do not commit, and do

  supplied code as given; no record identifies who chose them or why, so treat
  them as fixed inputs rather than as a decision open to revision here.

## Open questions and next actions

- Unknown: the intended consumer of the JSON output, and whether the
  inconsistent `surplus` key and `null` values are acceptable to it or need
  normalizing. This determines whether the parsing quirks above are features or
  defects; no next action is possible without the owner's answer.
- Unknown: whether the exit-1-with-traceback error behavior is acceptable, or
  whether the utility is expected to report a usage message for a missing
  argument.
- No test suite exists. Adding one is proposed, not approved, and would need to
  live outside the two preserved files.

- [`records.py`](records.py) — the entire implementation, 11 lines.
- [`samples/visits.csv`](samples/visits.csv) — fixture covering the parsing cases.

# Project context

Working notes on how `records.py` is invoked and how it treats input data. Everything
below was checked against the current `records.py` and `samples/visits.csv` by running
the utility; the observed output is quoted verbatim.

## Invocation

```
python3 records.py <path-to-csv>
```

- The input path is read from `sys.argv[1]`. It is the only input the program takes;
  there are no flags, no environment variables, and no configuration file.
- Result: a single line of JSON on stdout — an array of one object per data row —
  followed by a newline from `print`. Nothing is written to stderr on success, and
  nothing is written to disk.
- `json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False)` means non-ASCII characters are emitted as
  literal UTF-8 rather than `\uXXXX` escapes.
- Error behavior is whatever Python raises. Running with no argument raises
  `IndexError: list index out of range`; a missing file raises `FileNotFoundError`.
  Both surface as a traceback and a non-zero exit status. There is no argument
  validation or friendly error message, by design of the current script.

## Parsing rules

The file is opened with `newline=""` and `encoding="utf-8"` and handed to
`csv.DictReader` with `delimiter=";"` and `restkey="surplus"`. That fixes the
following behavior:

- **Semicolons, not commas, separate fields.** A comma is an ordinary character in a
  field.
- **The first line is the header** and supplies the object keys. Keys are used exactly
  as written — no trimming, lowercasing, or renaming.
- **Every value is a string.** `"12"` stays a string; nothing is coerced to a number,
  and `true` / `false` stay as text, not JSON booleans.
- **Standard CSV quoting applies.** Double quotes group a field, so `north;"a;b"`
  yields `{"site": "north", "note": "a;b"}`.
- **Blank lines are skipped** by `csv.DictReader` and produce no object.
- **`newline=""`** lets the `csv` module handle line endings itself, so `\r\n` input is
  parsed correctly rather than leaving stray `\r` in the last field.
- The whole file is materialized with `list(...)`, so memory use is proportional to
  input size. Fine for samples; worth knowing before pointing it at a large export.

## Row shape: the part that surprises people

Rows are not required to match the header width, and the two mismatch directions behave
differently. `samples/visits.csv` exists to pin down both:

```
site;visits;active
north;12;true
south;8
west;4;false;manual;checked
```

produces

```json
[{"site": "north", "visits": "12", "active": "true"},
 {"site": "south", "visits": "8", "active": null},
 {"site": "west", "visits": "4", "active": "false", "surplus": ["manual", "checked"]}]
```

- **Short row (`south`).** Missing trailing fields are filled with `DictReader`'s
  default `restval`, which is `None`, and serialize as JSON `null`. The key is still
  present. Consumers must distinguish "key absent" from "value is null" — here it is
  always the latter.
- **Long row (`west`).** Fields beyond the header are collected into a list under the
  `restkey`, `"surplus"`. So that one object has a key the others do not, and its value
  is an **array of strings**, not a string. Any consumer that assumes uniform keys or
  `str` values across records will break on this row.
- **Objects are therefore heterogeneous.** The JSON array is not a rectangular table.
  Treat the header keys as "usually present, possibly null" and `surplus` as
  "occasionally present, always a list".

`samples/visits.csv` is a fixture, not example data: each of its three rows covers one
case (exact width, short, long). Keep it byte-identical unless a behavior change
requires otherwise, and update this document in the same change if it does.

## Environment

Verified with the system `python3` (3.9.6 on this machine). The script uses only the
standard library — `csv`, `json`, `sys` — and no features newer than that, so any
supported Python 3 should behave the same.

## Known uncertainties

- Intended downstream consumer of the JSON is unknown, so whether `null` values and the
  `surplus` list are convenient or a problem for that consumer is an open question.
- The stringly-typed output (`"12"`, `"true"`) is recorded as observed behavior; whether
  callers are expected to coerce types themselves has not been confirmed.
- Duplicate header names and an empty input file behave predictably when tried outside
  this project — the last duplicate column wins (`site;site` / `a;b` yields
  `[{"site": "b"}]`), and an empty file yields `[]` — but no fixture here exercises
  them, so nothing guards against a future change to that behavior.
